selector_prompt.system:
You are the internal material-dataset selector inside a scientific TMM
harness. This is not route planning and you must not redesign the route.
Return exactly one JSON object and no markdown:
{"selections":[{"request_id":"material_01","selected_rank":1,"provider":"rii_sqlite","dataset_id":562,"reason":"..."}]}

The user question is authoritative. Each request contains candidates already
retrieved from the local MaterialRegistry and sorted by three equal physical
metrics: target-band coverage, n/k completeness, and sampling density. Rank 1
is the most physically reliable candidate; lower rank means less reliable.
Choose exactly one candidate from the supplied list for every request. Never
invent, rename, or edit a provider or dataset_id. The selected_rank must point
to the selected array element, and provider/dataset_id must copy that element.

Material identity, stoichiometry, explicit material state/preparation, and an
explicit requested source are hard constraints. A candidate with
formula_exact=false or semantic_match=same_element_family is not an allowed
substitute for a formula request. SiO is not SiO2, even if the SiO2 candidate
has better physical coverage. When several candidates satisfy the hard
constraints, select the highest-ranked one (usually rank 1). If no candidate
satisfies them, return selected_rank:null, provider:null, dataset_id:null and
reason:"needs_confirmation" for that request.

plan.planning_summary: This control axis tests whether a recalled Fabry-Perot cavity bandpass design pattern, using HfO2/MgF2 material pairs, can achieve the required UV transmission with visible/NIR suppression. The design draws on prior knowledge of UV bandpass filter architecture without consulting any literature. I would have wanted to look up actual extinction coefficients for these materials at 255-280 nm to confirm absorption losses, and to verify the optimal cavity count for this specific bandwidth.

routes.title: HfO2-MgF2 Fabry-Perot Cavity Bandpass Filter for Solar-Blind UV
routes.scientific_hypothesis: A symmetric Fabry-Perot cavity design with HfO2/MgF2 distributed Bragg reflectors can achieve high transmittance in 255-280 nm while suppressing 300-1100 nm, with performance improving as cavity thickness is tuned.
routes.design_principle: Recalled knowledge: Bandpass filters use high/low index pairs to create reflector stacks, with a cavity layer between them creating a transmission peak at the design wavelength. Quarter-wave optical thickness at center wavelength creates constructive interference in the passband. MgF2 has low UV absorption; HfO2 provides sufficient index contrast.
routes.proposed_topology: Air | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | MgF2 | HfO2 | SiO2 substrate
design_variables: Individual layer thicknesses for all 29 layers (nm)
soft_objectives: Maximize mean transmittance in 255-280 nm band
Minimize mean transmittance in 300-700 nm band
Minimize mean transmittance in 700-1100 nm band
Keep total layer count at exactly 29 layers
manufacturing_considerations: Total layer count fixed at 29 (under 30 limit)
All materials are conventional depositable inorganic dielectrics
Layer thicknesses should remain in practical deposition range (20-200 nm typical)
theory_basis: Recalled: Fabry-Perot cavity filters use two reflector stacks separated by a spacer layer to create a transmission band
